On November 8, 2004, the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), in collaboration with the Department of Health and Human Services and the Office of the Surgeon General, launched a free computer program called My Family Health Portrait. This tool allows individuals to document critical family health information, which can help identify hereditary patterns of common diseases. 2. On December 8, 2004, the NHGRI and the International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium announced the publication of a comparative analysis of the chicken and human genomes. This marked the first time a bird's genome had been sequenced and analyzed, with findings published in the December 9 issue of Nature. 3. On December 10, 2004, the International HapMap Consortium declared the removal of all restrictions on data generated from its efforts to map human genetic variation. This decision made the data fully accessible to the public, facilitating researchers' ability to identify genetic contributions to diseases. 4. On February 7, 2005, the International HapMap Consortium announced plans to create a more advanced map of human genetic variation than initially envisioned. This enhanced map aims to accelerate the discovery of genes associated with common diseases such as asthma, cancer, diabetes, and heart disease. 5. On March 16, 2005, as part of the Human Genome Project, the NIH celebrated the first comprehensive analysis of the human X chromosome sequence. This analysis provided groundbreaking insights into the evolution of sex chromosomes and the biological differences between males and females. 6. On August 8, 2005, the NHGRI announced the awarding of over $32 million in grants to advance the development of innovative DNA sequencing technologies. These technologies aim to reduce the cost of DNA sequencing and expand the application of genomics in biomedical research and healthcare. 7. On August 29, 2005, a research team led by the NHGRI discovered that a class of experimental anti-cancer drugs showed potential in laboratory studies for treating a fatal genetic disorder that causes premature aging. 8. On August 31, 2005, the first comprehensive comparison of the genetic blueprints of humans and chimpanzees revealed that our closest living relatives share 96% of our DNA sequence. 9. On October 5, 2005, the NIH announced contracts that would provide researchers with unprecedented access to two private collections of knockout mice. These resources offer valuable models for studying human diseases and lay the foundation for a public, genome-wide library of knockout mice. 10. On October 26, 2005, the International HapMap Consortium published a comprehensive catalog of human genetic variation. This milestone achievement is already accelerating the search for genes involved in common diseases such as asthma, diabetes, cancer, and heart disease. 11. On December 13, 2005, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and NHGRI launched a comprehensive initiative to advance the understanding of the molecular basis of cancer. This effort focuses on applying genome analysis technologies, particularly large-scale genome sequencing. 12. On February 8, 2006, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced two new initiatives aimed at accelerating research into the causes of common diseases such as asthma, arthritis, and Alzheimer’s disease. 13. On March 29, 2006, a multi-institution team of experts, coordinated by NHGRI geneticists, supported efforts to identify more than 70 unidentified bodies in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. 14. On July 18, 2006, researchers discovered that genetic alterations initially identified in individuals with a rare disease may also serve as a significant risk factor for the second most common form of dementia among the elderly. 15. On July 24, 2006, researchers at the NIH Chemical Genomics Center (NCGC), an NHGRI-affiliated center, developed a novel screening approach. This method profiles compounds in large chemical libraries with greater accuracy and precision than standard techniques, expediting the identification of biological activities and drug discovery leads. 16. On August 21, 2006, the NHGRI, part of the NIH, announced $54 million in grants over five years to establish a new Center of Excellence in Genomic Science (CEGS) and continue support for two existing centers. 17. On September 13, 2006, the NCI and NHGRI announced the first three cancers to be studied in the pilot phase of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). The cancers selected for study were lung, brain (glioblastoma), and ovarian cancers. 18. On October 4, 2006, the NHGRI announced a new round of grant awards totaling over $13 million to accelerate the development of innovative sequencing technologies. These technologies aim to reduce the cost of DNA sequencing and expand the use of genomics in medical research and healthcare. 19. On October 16, 2006, the NCI and NHGRI announced additional components of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Pilot Project. This three-year, $100 million collaboration aims to test the feasibility of using large-scale genome analysis technologies to identify critical genetic changes involved in cancer. 20. On November 15, 2006, new family health history projects were announced, focusing on Alaska Native and Appalachian communities. Acting Surgeon General Kenneth P. launched these outreach projects to educate Americans about the importance of understanding their family health histories. 21. On January 15, 2007, scientists identified a new genetic clue to the cause of Alzheimer’s disease. Variations in a gene known as SORL1 were found to potentially contribute to the development of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. 22. On April 26, 2007, researchers identified new genetic risk factors for type 2 diabetes. A Finnish team, working closely with two other groups, discovered at least four new genetic variants associated with an increased risk of diabetes and confirmed the existence of six others. 23. On May 4, 2007, the NHGRI and NCI partnered with Group Health Cooperative in Seattle and Henry Ford Health System in Detroit to launch the Multiplex Initiative. This study investigates the interest of healthy young adults in receiving genetic testing for eight common conditions.
